title: Egypt's Great Army Falls
overview: This chapter holds two poems announcing Egypt's defeat by Babylon, first in a famous battle far from home and then in Egypt itself, and it closes with a promise of rescue for Israel.

parts.label: Setting the scene (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: This opens a collection of messages about foreign nations, starting with Egypt, which Judah had often leaned on for help. Pharaoh Necho had killed Judah's king Josiah a few years before, and in 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon crushed his army at Carchemish, far north on the Euphrates River.

parts.label: Armed, then running (vv. 3-6)
parts.note: The poem mockingly calls the army to gear up, then suddenly shows the same soldiers panicking and fleeing. Neither speed nor strength saves them, and they fall far from home in the north.

parts.label: Rising like the Nile (vv. 7-12)
parts.note: Egypt's army swells like the Nile's yearly flood, boasting it will cover the earth, backed by hired troops from Cush, Put and Lud (scholars debate whether Lud means Lydia in modern Turkey or a people in Africa). The poem bluntly pictures the slaughter as a sacrifice belonging to the LORD, and says not even Gilead's famous healing balm can cure this wound.

parts.label: Invasion of Egypt itself (vv. 13-19)
parts.note: A later message warns that Nebuchadnezzar will reach Egypt's own cities, its hired soldiers will run home, and Pharaoh will be mocked as all noise and no action. The coming conqueror towers like Mount Tabor and Mount Carmel, though historians are unsure how far Babylon's actual invasion went.

parts.label: Heifer, snake and forest (vv. 20-26)
parts.note: Egypt is pictured as a sleek young cow stung by a fly from the north, a snake hissing as it slips away, and a dense forest cut down by woodcutters. The judgment reaches even Amon, the chief god of Thebes, yet it ends with a promise that Egypt will be lived in again.

parts.label: Comfort for Israel (vv. 27-28)
parts.note: These lines, which also appear earlier in the book, tell scattered Israel not to fear because they will be brought home. Israel will still be corrected, but only in fair measure and never wiped out.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether these poems should be read as detailed predictions spoken long before the events or as poetic messages shaped around events already unfolding.
think: When a nation or person seems unstoppable, what do you think actually decides whether that power lasts or falls?
